articles.excerpt: Two exports both say October. One is a merchant's monthly processing statement. The other is an activity report filtered by settlement date. Your importer gives them the same 2026-10 key, joins the to…
articles.body: Two exports both say October. One is a merchant's monthly processing statement. The other is an activity report filtered by settlement date. Your importer gives them the same 2026-10 key, joins the totals, and raises a discrepancy. The files may be correct. The comparison contract may be missing. I work on BrowserAct. A guide we prepared about Worldpay iQ statements separates monthly processing statements, activity reports, and other financial records. For a developer, that distinction should survive ingestion. A human-readable month label cannot express which event date selected the underlying records. This article proposes an application-side review gate for document metadata. The example uses fictional merchants and synthetic records.

articles.title: Your RAG Index Is Already Out of Date: Building an Incremental Ingestion Pipeline
articles.excerpt: Most retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tutorials end at the same point: load some documents, split them into chunks, embed them, store them in a vector database and ask questions. That is enough fo…
articles.body: Most retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tutorials end at the same point: load some documents, split them into chunks, embed them, store them in a vector database and ask questions. That is enough for a demo. It is not enough for a system that a business relies on, because real documents change every day. Policies get revised, product pages get updated, a contract gets replaced and an old one should no longer be quoted. If your index does not reflect those changes, your assistant will confidently answer with yesterday's facts. In my experience, stale or duplicated chunks cause more wrong answers than the language model itself. The quick fix teams usually try is to rebuild the whole index every night.

articles.title: The Tool-Design Mistakes That Make AI Agents Unreliable
articles.excerpt: The Tool-Design Mistakes That Make AI Agents Unreliable A lot of "the model is unreliable" complaints are actually tool-design problems. The model is doing exactly what an ambiguous or overloaded tool…
articles.body: The Tool-Design Mistakes That Make AI Agents Unreliable A lot of "the model is unreliable" complaints are actually tool-design problems. The model is doing exactly what an ambiguous or overloaded tool definition told it to do. 🧰 One Tool Doing Too Many Things A single tool with a dozen optional parameters covering unrelated use cases forces the model to guess which combination applies. Splitting it into several narrow, clearly-named tools removes the guesswork entirely. 📝 Descriptions That Don't Say When to Use It A tool description that only explains what a tool does, not when to use it versus a similar tool, leaves the model to infer the boundary — and it infers wrong often enough to matter at scale.
articles.author: klyx

articles.title: Check that a research CSV join preserves one row per participant
articles.excerpt: A row count can stay the same even when a merge drops one participant and duplicates another. If your analysis expects one row per participant, compare the identifier counts before and after the join.…
articles.body: A row count can stay the same even when a merge drops one participant and duplicates another. If your analysis expects one row per participant, compare the identifier counts before and after the join. This example uses fictional identifiers. The two files have the same number of rows, but the second file lost P03 and has an extra P02. from collections import Counter before = Counter ( [ "P01" , "P02" , "P03" ] ) after = Counter ( [ "P01" , "P02" , "P02" ] ) lost = before - after extra = after - before assert sum ( before . values ( ) ) == sum ( after . values ( ) ) == 3 assert dict ( lost ) == { "P03" : 1 } assert dict ( extra ) == { "P02" : 1 } print ( f "Lost rows: {dict(lost)}" ) print ( f "Extra rows: {dict(extra)}" ) The output is Lost rows: {'P03': 1} and Extra rows: {'P02': 1} .

articles.body: Although I no longer use it, there’s little doubt in my mind that Nova Launcher is a titan of the Android customization space. articles.excerpt: SpaceX has moved its Starship Super Heavy booster to the pad to prep for the next test flight of the megarocket, a historic mission scheduled to launch this Friday (Nov. 13).
articles.body: SpaceX is one big step closer to the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket. The company announced today (Nov. 10) that it had moved its latest Starship first stage, known as Super Heavy Booster 22, to the launch mount at its Starbase facility in South Texas ahead of Flight 15, which is scheduled to lift off this Friday (Nov. 13). During the upcoming launch test, SpaceX plans to catch both Booster 22 and Starship's Ship upper stage with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms in a double landing catch — something the private spaceflight company has never tried before. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. SpaceX's Flight 15 Starship Super Heavy booster in its assembly bay, before its move to Starbase's launch mount.

articles.body: In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "Wolverine") attached would elicit intense fan interest, but add the superstar vocal talents of Anthony Mackie ("Avengers: Infinity War," "Avengers: Doomsday"), Ariana DeBose ("West Side Story"), and John Leguizamo ("Ice Age"), and it catapults this sonic odyssey into the stratosphere. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 10, 2013: Europe's GOCE satellite, the 'Ferrari of space,' fell out of orbit after mapping Earth's gravity field
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel . At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth . Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage. It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected.

articles.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
articles.excerpt: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
articles.body: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

articles.title: A distant exoplanet mysteriously vanished from sight. Astronomers just discovered why
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an exoplanet that "disappeared" after seven years of observations.
articles.body: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, that "disappeared" after seven years of observations. New research suggests that the planet hasn't vanished at all, but has been dragged off its orbit by an unseen planet. The exoplanet , designated TOI-2535 b, is located around 1,000 light-years away. TOI-2535 b was routinely observed with NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite ( TESS ) space telescope for seven years between April 2019 and March 2026 as it completed its 8.25-Earth day orbit of its parent star. That's 10 times quicker than the orbit of Mercury around the sun and means this blisteringly hot planet is classed as a " hot Jupiter ." However, something strange happened started to happen as astronomers observed the distant world.
